competency.competency_text: Comprehend and interpret primary cultural source material

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret a primary cultural text to draw conclusions about the values and worldview it encodes
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Vedas and Vedic Culture — a. What are the Vedas?
assessment_items.question_text: The Rig Veda contains the line: 'The Existent is one, but sages give it many names' (ekam sat viprā bahudhā vadanti). A student reads this line and concludes: 'The early Vedic thinkers were not polytheists who believed in many separate gods — they saw all deities as expressions of one reality.' Which feature of the line best supports this conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: The line appears in the Rig Veda, the first of the four Vedas, so it represents the most important Vedic belief.

options.label: B
options.text: The line is written in early Sanskrit, which shows it is an ancient and therefore authoritative source.

options.label: C
options.text: The line mentions sages, which proves that only trained scholars could understand Vedic religion.

options.label: D
options.text: The line says the Existent is one — a single reality — even though sages name it many ways, implying the many deities are different names for one truth.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Mistakes language of composition for interpretive content — age and authority of a source is not the same as what the source says; this reveals confusion between source critique and source interpretation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Over-reads the mention of 'sages' — the line uses sages to make a claim about multiple names for one reality, not to restrict access to religious knowledge.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses position in a list with interpretive significance — the chapter does not rank the four Vedas by importance; this reveals a misunderstanding of how to use textual evidence.

competency.competency_text: Comprehend and interpret primary cultural source material

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret a primary cultural text to draw conclusions about the values and worldview it encodes
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Vedas and Vedic Culture — a. What are the Vedas?
assessment_items.question_text: The last mantras of the Rig Veda call for unity among people. A teacher says: 'This shows that the value of unity was not just a social preference — it was built into the most sacred texts of Vedic culture.' Which of the following best evaluates the teacher's claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct because the Rig Veda is the oldest of the four Vedas, making its values more important than those of the others.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is supported — placing a call for unity in the closing mantras of the Rig Veda gives it structural emphasis within a sacred text, suggesting it was a core value.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is too strong — we cannot know what the composers meant, because the Vedas were oral texts.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is unsupported — unity appears only in the last mantras, so it was probably added later and is not a core Vedic value.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Misapplies a source-critique concern — oral transmission does not mean we cannot interpret a text's content; it is a non-sequitur objection that mistakes the transmission method for interpretive inaccessibility.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies a false logic — placing something at the end of a text can signal culminating importance, not later addition; this distractor reveals confusion about how textual position functions as evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reintroduces the ranking fallacy — the chapter does not rank the four Vedas by importance; age of composition is not the same as weight of value.

competency.competency_text: Appreciate India's tradition of inclusion and mutual enrichment across communities

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse specific historical examples to demonstrate that cultural exchange between communities was bidirectional rather than one-directional
assessment_items.chapter_section: Folk and Tribal Roots — mutual interaction: Jagannath, tribal epics, shared sacred concepts
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that sociologist André Béteille argued tribal religions and Hinduism have each shaped the other throughout history. Which pair of examples from the chapter best illustrates that this exchange was bidirectional — flowing in both directions?

options.label: A
options.text: Jagannath of Puri is believed to have originally been a tribal deity absorbed into Hinduism; some tribes developed their own versions of the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa.

options.label: B
options.text: Jainism spread through rock-cut caves; Buddhism spread through the Sangha.

options.label: C
options.text: The Buddha taught ahimsa; Jain monks also practised ahimsa.

options.label: D
options.text: The Vedic tradition named over thirty clans; tribal communities also organised themselves into clans.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Draws on a different section of the chapter (Buddhist and Jain spread) and does not address tribal-Hindu exchange at all — reveals confusion about which traditions the question concerns.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Identifies a structural parallel (both had clans) rather than an exchange — parallel organisation does not constitute bidirectional cultural influence.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Draws on Buddhist and Jain sections and again does not address tribal-Hindu exchange — reveals an inability to locate the relevant section of the chapter.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why the abandonment of earlier reductive descriptions of tribal communities reflects a more accurate understanding of India's social history
assessment_items.chapter_section: Folk and Tribal Roots — What is a tribe?
assessment_items.question_text: Earlier anthropologists described tribal communities as 'primitive'. The chapter says this description has been largely abandoned with deeper study. Which of the following best explains why abandoning this description matters for understanding Indian history?

options.label: A
options.text: It allows us to use more polite language when discussing tribal communities in school.

options.label: B
options.text: It proves that tribal communities are now more developed than they were in ancient times.

options.label: C
options.text: It recognises that tribal communities, like other janas, had their own cultures, governance, and belief systems — making them integral parts of India's history rather than marginal groups.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that ancient India had a single, unified culture shared equally by all communities.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reduces the issue to politeness rather than historical accuracy — misses the chapter's argument that the change reflects a substantive correction to how tribal communities are understood as historical actors.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a developmental-progress framing the chapter explicitly rejects — 'more developed than before' reinstates the very hierarchy the abandonment of 'primitive' was meant to correct.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Contradicts the chapter's central argument — the chapter consistently argues for diversity and mutual exchange, not a single unified culture; this distractor reveals a fundamental misreading of the chapter's claim.

competency.competency_text: Recognise India's contributions to humanity through the spread of philosophical, ethical, and cultural ideas

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why a specific Indian cultural practice constitutes a contribution to humanity's shared heritage
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Vedas and Vedic Culture — a. What are the Vedas?
assessment_items.question_text: In 2008, UNESCO recognised Vedic chanting as 'a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity'. Which of the following best explains why UNESCO described Vedic chanting as a contribution to humanity rather than just to India?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the Vedas contain scientific knowledge that is useful for people in every country.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the Vedic hymns were composed in Sanskrit, which is the mother of all world languages.

options.label: C
options.text: Because UNESCO recognised it, and UNESCO only recognises things that are popular across all countries.

options.label: D
options.text: Because Vedic chanting demonstrates that a sophisticated body of knowledge can be transmitted without writing across 100–200 generations, showing humanity a method of preserving intangible heritage.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a claim not made in the chapter — the chapter does not state Sanskrit is the mother of all world languages; this distractor tests whether students import outside knowledge that the chapter does not support.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a claim about scientific content the chapter does not make — the chapter focuses on the method of oral transmission and the values encoded in the hymns, not on scientific utility.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Circular reasoning — uses UNESCO recognition to justify UNESCO recognition; also factually misstates how UNESCO makes decisions; reveals an inability to evaluate the reason behind a recognition.

competency.competency_text: Recognise India's contributions to humanity through the spread of philosophical, ethical, and cultural ideas

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how Indian philosophical teachings spread beyond India and assess the significance of that diffusion
assessment_items.chapter_section: Buddhism — Jātaka tales and the Buddha's influence
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter says the Buddha's influence on India and Asia was enormous and remains perceptible today. Which of the following best explains how the Jātaka tales contributed to Buddhism's spread beyond India?

options.label: A
options.text: The Jātaka tales contained political instructions that helped Buddhist rulers govern their kingdoms.

options.label: B
options.text: The Jātaka tales taught Buddhist values — such as ahimsa, duty, and self-sacrifice — through memorable narratives that could be shared orally across communities and regions.

options.label: C
options.text: The Jātaka tales were stored in rock-cut caves, which preserved them for future generations to find.

options.label: D
options.text: The Jātaka tales were translated into Sanskrit and distributed by the Vedic tradition across the subcontinent.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes the spread to the Vedic tradition — directly contradicts the chapter's framing of Buddhism as departing from Vedic authority; reveals confusion about which tradition was responsible for Buddhist transmission.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reduces the Jātaka tales to political utility — the chapter presents them as moral-values narratives, not governance manuals; this reveals a misreading of the tales' purpose.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates the Jātaka tales with the physical infrastructure of rock-cut caves — the caves were associated with Jain and Buddhist monks' residences, not specifically with the storage of the Jātaka tales as texts.
